facts.claim: "Just In Time" was produced by Christo and Monte Booker.
The song was written by Christo, JID, Kenny Mason, Lil Wayne and Monte Booker.
Kenny Mason performs the chorus. The Lil Wayne fan wiki credits him with lead vocals and writing, Wayne with featured vocals and writing, and John Kadadu with recording.
On The Breakfast Club, JID said he did not hear Lil Wayne's verse on "Just In Time" until mixing began.
JID told The Breakfast Club he was booed on a small 2016 college run opening for Lil Wayne, because Wayne was late.
The track is the 12th song on The Forever Story, which was released August 26, 2022 on Dreamville/Interscope. The "Extended Version" listing is a later release.
The Forever Story was executive produced by longtime JID collaborator Christo. Kenny Mason also appears on the album's single "Dance Now".

The Forever Story is JID's third studio album. It was recorded over about two years, starting in March 2020 at the Spillage Village studio house in Atlanta. It is conceptually a sequel to his 2017 debut The Never Story.
One review says the track shows JID's reverence for the craft and pairs him with Lil Wayne, one of his heroes who is now a peer.
JID (Destin Choice Route) is an Atlanta rapper and a member of Spillage Village. He is signed to J. Cole's Dreamville and to Interscope, and his lyrics draw on his upbringing in East Atlanta.

research.lineage: The song sits in Atlanta lyric-driven Southern hip-hop and the Dreamville/Spillage Village orbit, and it pairs JID with Lil Wayne, a New Orleans rap veteran.

draft:
The first thing anyone in **Just In Time** does after waking up is pray, and the prayer goes to a gun. Kenny Mason's chorus opens on "Woke up at six, pray to a .9," then keeps doubling its own numbers: six, twelve, the age a kid was already running from the police. From there it turns to a boast that sounds more like a dare: I got the time today. On a song this crowded with clock talk, that claim carries weight. Time here means danger, punishment, and survival. Having any to spare is the flex.

The verses work every idiom the word allows. They kill time, do time, get handed more time, and put in time since the beginning of it. It plays as a dazzling game, and it's meant to. But the wordplay keeps snagging on memory. In the middle of the swagger comes a scene that lands harder than any punchline: "Ma would go inside behind the window, hide." The line stays short and gives no detail beyond the hiding. Then, a few bars later: "God left when the winter came, then the summer died." Two seasons gone, with no one to answer for it. The pride and the fear sit side by side and never settle. The song brags about having all the time in the world because it remembers a house where nobody could count on any.

Christo and Monte Booker built the track lean and dry. A distorted bass loops a short, stubborn pattern. A drum machine drives a medium-fast beat with a snapping snare and busy hi-hats, and a synth pad holds bright chords overhead. There's barely any reverb, so every syllable hits close and clean. The groove has a slight bounce, enough to keep the menace light on its feet, and the rapping rides it fast and clear, with no harmonies softening anything.

The title carries an irony the record never says out loud. JID told The Breakfast Club he got booed on a 2016 college run opening for Lil Wayne, because Wayne was late. Six years later Wayne shows up on JID's third album, and JID said he didn't hear the verse until mixing began. One review put it this way: a hero who's now a peer. It's the 12th track on The Forever Story, the sequel to his 2017 debut The Never Story, recorded largely at the Spillage Village house in Atlanta. Its East Atlanta memories run through the same lyric-first Southern lineage that made a New Orleans veteran the right guest.

The song keeps telling you it has all the time in the world, and the more it insists, the more you hear how close a few of those years came to running out.
